I'd pick **candidate 1**. This comes from rough reasoning in my head, not a simulation, so treat it as a judgement call.

1. **Order every day, not in batches.** Candidate 7 orders both goods every other day in double amounts. That saves the 21 fee on about 13 days, roughly 273 in total. But it means about 65 extra in storage cost per two-day pair and more pressure on the 252-unit limit, so it loses more than it saves. Candidate 0 still orders something every day, so it saves no fees, and batching good 1 only adds storage cost.

2. **The other plans differ only in how far they order above forecast.** Candidates 1–6 all order each good's forecast for the day it arrives, times a fixed factor:

   | Candidate | Good 0 | Good 1 |
   |---|---|---|
   | 5 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
   | 3 | 1.1 | 1.1 |
   | 1 | 1.15 | 1.15 |
   | 2 | 1.2 | 1.2 |
   | 6 | 1.3 | 1.1 |
   | 4 | 1.3 | 1.3 |

3. **Choosing the factor.** Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, and on good 0 a day's demand swings by about ±11 units.
   - Ordering at 1.0 runs short too often. A missed sale costs 11 on good 0 (7 lost margin plus 4 penalty) and 9 on good 1.
   - Leftovers carry over to the next day, so a moderate surplus acts as a cheap buffer: storage is only 0.7–0.9 per unit per day.
   - At 1.2–1.3 the surplus piles up. Good 0 starts spoiling after 4 days (each spoiled unit wastes 12 plus storage), the combined stock hits the 252 limit, and whatever is left at day 29 is worth nothing.
   - The best point is a little above average demand, about 1.1–1.15. Candidate 1's 1.15 builds a buffer without wasting much stock. Candidate 3 (1.1) is the close runner-up.

I pick **candidate 5**, with moderate confidence. The comparison was done in my head with rough approximations of the randomness, not a full simulation. Candidate 3 is a close second.

**What the candidates are.** Candidates 1–6 order every day, each a fixed multiple of the forecast demand for the day the order arrives:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ≈1.00 | ≈1.00 |
| 3 | ≈1.10 | ≈1.10 |
| 1 | ≈1.15 | ≈1.15 |
| 2 | ≈1.19 | ≈1.19 |
| 6 | ≈1.30 | ≈1.10 |
| 4 | ≈1.30 | ≈1.30 |

Candidates 0 and 7 order every other day, combining two days into one order.

**Why every-other-day ordering loses.**
- Candidate 7 skips about 14 order days and saves about 21 × 14 ≈ 294 in order fees. But each two-day batch holds roughly half its quantity for an extra night. That costs about 40 × 0.7 + 40 × 0.9 ≈ 64 per pair of days, against 21 saved. Large batches can also overflow the 252-unit warehouse.
- Candidate 0 still orders product 0 every day, so it saves nothing on fees. It only adds extra holding cost for product 1, so it is worse than candidate 1.

**Why ordering above forecast loses.** The plan is fixed in advance and cannot react to actual sales. So any amount ordered above the average actual demand (the forecast × 1.046) piles up day after day. It then either spoils or is held at a cost, and stock left at the end is worth nothing.
- **Product 0** (approx. 28 days × ~39 units, daily spread ≈ 13):
  - Raising the multiple by 0.05 costs about 12 × 0.05 × 1092 ≈ 655 in extra purchases, plus more holding cost.
  - It cuts lost sales by only about 20–30 units. Each lost unit costs 19 revenue + 4 penalty = 23, so that saves about 500–700.
  - My estimated total costs: about 15 450 at 1.00, 15 600 at 1.05, 16 000 at 1.10 and 16 800 at 1.15. Lower is better.
- **Product 1:**
  - Going from 1.00 to 1.10 adds about 430 in purchases and about 450 in holding cost.
  - It saves about 630 in lost sales (14 per unit).
  - The net is about −250, so 1.00 is better.
- **Start of the month:** the opening shortfall (product 0 on day 1, product 1 on days 0–4) is the same for every candidate, so it doesn't change the ranking.

**Robustness to randomness.** Higher multiples add steady losses from overstock and holding no matter how demand turns out. Their benefit only appears when demand is unusually high. With actual demand spreading about ±30% around the forecast, the 1.00 plan comes out ahead on expected profit.

I picked **candidate 3**. I estimated this in my head rather than simulating it, so it's a judgement call, not a calculated result.

1. **Candidates 1–6 are the same plan scaled up or down.** Candidate 1 orders about 1.15× the forecast for the day each order arrives. That is about 1.1× the expected demand, because the multiplier averages about 1.046. Candidate 3 is about 1.04× expected demand. Candidate 5 is slightly below it, at about 0.96×. Candidates 2, 4 and 6 order more than candidate 1.

2. **Ordering above demand loses money.** Unsold stock carries over to later days, and items are sold oldest first. So a steady surplus mostly ends up as stock that is worthless at the end. Each extra unit costs its purchase price (12 for product 0) plus about 10 in storage over the rest of the month. A unit short costs only about 11 (the lost margin plus the penalty). Going from candidate 3 up to candidate 1 adds roughly 80 units of product 0 for about 1,700 extra cost. It saves only a few hundred in shortages.

3. **Ordering below demand also loses money.** At candidate 5's level, stock hovers near zero. Shortages then cost about 11 per unit for product 0 and 9 for product 1, which outweighs the purchases saved. Candidate 3 adds just enough margin to make up the early shortage from the low starting stock and to cover random demand swings.

4. **Candidates 0 and 7 batch orders.** Candidate 0 orders product 1 every other day but still pays the 21 fee daily, so it saves nothing and pays more storage. Candidate 7 does save 21 for every two days. But it holds about one extra day of both products overnight, costing about 60 in storage, and it risks overflowing the 252-unit warehouse.

I pick **candidate 3** (choice = 3). My confidence is moderate, not high. This is a mental estimate on average values, not a step-by-step simulation.

1. **Candidates 0 and 7 lose.** Candidate 0 still orders item 0 every day, so it saves no ordering fees, and doubling up item 1 only adds holding cost. Candidate 7 saves about 13 × 21 ≈ 273 in fees. But the extra day of storage for each doubled batch costs about 770 (roughly 340 for item 0 and 430 for item 1). Avoiding a few shortages doesn't make up the gap.

2. **The daily-order plans differ only in scale.** Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.
   - Item 0: forecast total ≈ 1177, expected ≈ 1231.
   - Item 1: forecast for days 5–29 is 945, expected ≈ 988. Shortages in days 1–4 are the same for every plan.

   How much each plan delivers compared with that:

   | Candidate | Item 0 (incl. start stock) | Item 1 (days 5–29) | Verdict |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 5 | ≈ −80 | — | Systematic shortage: lost sales ≈ 90 × 23 outweigh the ≈1236 saved on purchases |
   | 3 | ≈ +22 | ≈ +52 | Best balance |
   | 1 | ≈ +91 | ≈ +99 | Too much surplus |
   | 2 | ≈ +142 | ≈ +148 | Too much surplus |
   | 4, 6 | ≈ +250 | — | Excess item 0, very costly |

3. **Why bigger surpluses lose.** Shelf life (4 and 6 days) and FIFO mean little spoils over the 30 days. Instead, the extra stock piles up as a buffer: you pay holding on it every day, and whatever is left at the end is a total loss. Daily demand swings are about 11 units for each item. So candidate 3's small upward drift already keeps shortages near a few dozen units.

4. **Comparing 1 with 3.** Candidate 1 buys about 69 more units of item 0 (≈828) and about 47 more of item 1 (≈235). On top of that comes roughly +700 and +560 in holding. All this saves only about 20 + 10 units of shortage, worth ≈ 600. So candidate 3 comes out ahead. Candidates 4 and 6 lose even more for the same reason.

I pick **candidate 5**. I worked this out by hand, so it is a rough estimate rather than a precise calculation.

**What all candidates share.** The starting stock can't cover the first few days. Product 0 has 50 units against about 71 units of demand on days 0–1. Product 1 has 45 units against about 155 units on days 0–4, before its first order arrives. These shortfalls are the same in every plan, so they don't separate the candidates.

**How the six daily-order plans differ.** Candidates 1–6 order every day in amounts scaled to the forecast for the arrival day. The scale is about 1.0 for candidate 5, about 1.1 for 3 (and for product 1 in candidate 6), about 1.15 for 1, about 1.2 for 2, and about 1.3 for 4 (and for product 0 in candidate 6). Expected demand is about 1.046 × forecast. So candidate 5 under-orders by about 4–5% per day, and every other plan over-orders.

**What over-ordering costs.** Unsold stock carries over to the next day, so any extra builds up as a growing buffer, which I treated as a random walk with drift:
- Holding cost grows roughly with the square of the horizon: 0.7–0.9 per unit per day over about 28 days.
- Whatever is left at the end is bought and lost: 12 per unit of product 0, 5 per unit of product 1.
- Daily demand varies by about ±12 units, so random swings already create a buffer of roughly 35–50 units even with no drift. That buffer prevents most stockouts. Pushing it higher saves little on shortages and costs a lot in holding and leftover stock.

**Rough comparison (product 0, losses relative to a perfect plan):**
- Drift −1.8 per day (candidate 5): about −1845
- No drift: about −1840
- Drift +1.7 per day (candidate 3): about −2150

Higher scales lose even more. For product 1, the plans at −1.8 and 0 drift come out about equal, and +1.7 is worse (about −1790 against −1570). Candidates 1, 2, 4 and 6 are clearly worse because of holding costs and leftover stock.

**Batched plans.**
- Candidate 0 matches candidate 1 for product 0 and orders product 1 every other day in double amounts. Product 0 is still ordered daily, so it saves no daily order fees and only adds holding cost.
- Candidate 7 batches both products every other day. That saves about 270 in order fees but adds about 340 in product 0 holding, on top of a buffer that is already too large.

**Robustness.** If demand comes in below forecast, the plans that over-order lose the most. Candidate 5 holds the least stock and the smallest final leftover. On my estimate it is close to tied with the zero-drift case and ahead of everything else.

**Answer: candidate 3.** I worked this out by reasoning with rough estimates, not by simulating each plan.

**How the plans differ.** Candidates 1–6 all order every day with the same daily pattern. They differ only by a scaling factor relative to the forecast:
- Candidate 1: about 1.15 × forecast.
- Candidate 2: about 1.20 × forecast.
- Candidate 3: about 1.09 × forecast.
- Candidate 4: about 1.30 × forecast.
- Candidate 5: about 1.00 × forecast.
- Candidate 6: about 1.30 for product 0 and about 1.09 for product 1.

Candidates 0 and 7 batch their orders every two days.

**Where the losses come from.** Average actual demand is about 1.046 × forecast. Leftover stock carries over to the next day, and sales take the oldest stock first. So any steady over-ordering piles up until it spoils. In the meantime it costs storage every day, and the pile grows toward the shelf-life limit. For example, product 0 at ×1.15 heads toward roughly 3 × 43 ≈ 130 units.
- **Candidates 4 and 6:** product 0 is ordered about 25 % above average demand. That means roughly 9 units/day written off at 12 each, plus storage on a large stock. Candidate 4 does the same for product 1 too, and the combined stock can exceed the 252-unit warehouse limit, so part of each delivery is lost. These are clearly the worst.
- **Candidate 2, and to a lesser extent candidate 1:** the same effect on a smaller scale. Under my estimate, storage plus write-offs cost more than the shortages they prevent.
- **Candidate 5:** orders about 4.6 % below average demand. That means a steady shortage, costing 11 per unit for product 0 and 9 for product 1. Random swings add further shortages on top.
- **Candidates 0 and 7:** ordering every other day makes each delivery twice as large, so average stock is about half a day's demand higher. The extra storage costs about 350–500 per product over the period. Candidate 7 saves about 250 in order fees by ordering half as often. Candidate 0 saves almost nothing, because it still orders product 0 every day. Both also scale around ×1.15, like candidate 1.

**Under random demand.** Candidate 3 orders about 4 % above average demand. This small margin absorbs random dips and spikes: leftover stock usually sells within the shelf life (4 days for product 0, 6 for product 1). Storage stays moderate and write-offs stay small. Keeping a small surplus costs less than running a small shortage, so candidate 3 beats candidate 5.

Candidate 1 is the closest rival. My comparison between 1 and 3 is approximate and could go either way. The ranking I'm confident in is that ×1.30 and the batching plans come out worse.

I'd pick **candidate 1**. I estimated this in my head, not by simulation, and it's close between candidates 1, 2 and 3.

1. **Daily orders beat ordering every other day (rules out 0 and 7).** Candidate 7 is candidate 1 with each two days' orders combined into one. Skipping a day saves the 21 order fee. But that day's goods then sit on the shelf an extra night. That costs about 36 × 0.7 + 40 × 0.9 ≈ 61, which is more than the 21 saved. Candidate 0 still orders product 0 every day, so it pays the fee daily anyway, and its product 1 batches add the same extra holding.

2. **Size of the daily orders.** Candidates 1–6 all order the forecast for the day the goods arrive, times a fixed factor:

| Candidate | Product 0 factor | Product 1 factor |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 3 | 1.1 | 1.1 |
| 1 | 1.15 | 1.15 |
| 2 | 1.2 | 1.2 |
| 6 | 1.3 | 1.1 |
| 4 | 1.3 | 1.3 |

   - The plan is fixed and can't react to actual demand. Its only protection against a high-demand day is stock left over from earlier days.
   - Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, so candidate 5 runs slightly short on average and will often have unmet demand.

A unit short costs the lost margin plus the penalty: 11 for product 0, 9 for product 1. So for product 0 it only pays to over-order a little. Product 1 (cheaper to waste, 6-day shelf life) can take a bit more.
   - Both 1.3 factors (candidates 4 and 6) build up a lot of product 0 that spoils. At 1.1 (candidate 3) the stock buffer grows slowly and often runs out.
   - About 15% above forecast (candidate 1) looks like the best balance. Candidate 2 (1.2) is close behind.

**Choice: candidate 5** — the plan that orders right at the forecast (multiplier ≈ 1.0). I did this as a rough mental estimate of averages with a random-walk approximation, not a simulation, so my confidence is moderate.

**Candidate structure.** Candidates 1–6 order every day and track the forecast for the arrival day. They differ only in how far they order above it. Candidate 5 orders about 1.0× the forecast, candidate 3 about 1.09×, candidate 1 about 1.16×, candidate 2 about 1.2×, candidate 4 about 1.3×, and candidate 6 about 1.3× for item 0 and 1.1× for item 1. Candidates 0 and 7 have the volume of candidate 1 but bunch orders every other day: item 1 only in candidate 0, both items in candidate 7.

**Why ordering above the forecast loses.** The orders are fixed in advance, so stock behaves like a random walk. Daily demand varies by about ±11 units on each item. Each extra unit of daily excess adds a drift that compounds over 28 days:
- **Item 0.** Profit ≈ 7·D − 12·(excess bought) − 23·(lost units) − holding. Each extra unit per day of excess costs about 336 over the period. The buffer that builds up costs about 0.7 per unit per day to hold. Fewer stockouts do not pay for this. My estimates of total losses: about 1,450–1,550 at 1.0–1.05×, about 2,150 at 1.09×, more at 1.16×, and much more at 1.3×, where many units also spoil.
- **Item 1.** The same picture: about 860 at 1.0×, about 1,140 at 1.05×, and about 1,775 at 1.1×. Holding at 0.9 per unit per day dominates.
- **The start is the same for everyone.** In the first days (item 0 on day 1, item 1 on days 0–4) nothing has arrived yet, so the shortage is identical for all plans and does not change the ranking.

**Why bunching loses.** Ordering every other day saves about 14 × 21 ≈ 294 in fixed order fees. But half of each batch sits an extra night: about 350 extra holding for item 0 and about 430 for item 1. So candidate 7 is worse than daily orders. Candidate 0 also orders item 0 every day, so it saves no fees at all and only adds holding for item 1.

**Robustness.** With lower ordering, a demand drop costs less: less waste and less holding. A demand spike costs about 11 per missing unit for item 0 and about 9 for item 1. The higher plans pay for every deviation through waste and holding, in both directions.

I'd pick **Candidate 1**. I compared the plans by rough mental estimates, not by simulating them, so this is my best judgement rather than a confirmed result.

1. **Rule out the batched plans (0 and 7).** Candidate 7 orders every other day, which saves about 13 order fees of 21 each, roughly 273. 2. **Compare the daily plans (1–6) by order size.** They differ only by how much they scale up the forecast:
   - Candidate 5: about 1.0×

2. **Кандидат 7 — это кандидат 1, где заказы двух дней объединены в один.** Так он экономит около 15 фиксированных платежей по 21. Но половина каждой партии лежит на складе лишнюю ночь: это примерно 40 × 0,7 по товару 0 и 40 × 0,9 по товару 1, то есть около 64 за пару дней против 21 экономии. 3. **Масштаб.** Заказы не зависят от фактического спроса, а излишки переходят на следующие дни, пока не истечёт годность. Поэтому важно, чтобы средний объём заказа шёл чуть выше среднего спроса (около 1,046 × прогноз).
   - Масштаб 1,00 ниже этого уровня, и нехватка повторяется постоянно. Каждая недостающая единица стоит 7 + 4 = 11 по товару 0 и 6 + 3 = 9 по товару 1.

   - Небольшой перевес над средним спросом даёт запас на случай колебаний и почти без списаний. На мой взгляд, 1,09–1,10 у кандидата 3 лучше, чем 1,15 у кандидата 1, у которого постоянного списания больше. Однако разница между ними невелика, и по одной прикидке я не могу это подтвердить.

Candidate 5 orders about 1.0× the forecast, 3 about 1.1×, 1 about 1.15×, 2 about 1.2× and 4 about 1.3×. Candidate 6 orders about 1.3× for product 0 and 1.1× for product 1.
- Candidate 0 matches candidate 1 for product 0 but orders product 1 every other day. It still pays the 21 fee every day because product 0 is ordered daily, so batching only adds holding cost. It is worse than candidate 1.

But holding the larger batches costs about 64 extra per two days (about 28 for product 0 and 36 for product 1), which is more than the 21 saved. It is also more likely to hit the 252-unit capacity.

**Why ordering above average demand loses:** average demand is about 1.046× the forecast. Any plan that orders more than that keeps adding stock. Day-to-day swings don't use it up, so the stock grows until batches start expiring:
- **Product 1** keeps for 6 days, so excess can pile up to about 5 days of stock, roughly 150 units. Holding that costs about 0.9 × 150 ≈ 135 a day. At 1.0× the backlog averages about 35 units, or roughly 31 a day.
- **Product 0** keeps for 4 days. At 1.1× or more, about 2 or more units a day expire (at least 24 a day lost), plus higher holding.
- **At 1.0×** about 1.6–1.9 units of demand per product go unmet each day, costing roughly 14–21 a day per product in lost margin and penalties. That is clearly less than the cost of overstocking.

Higher order levels mainly add stock that costs holding or expires. Candidate 6 overstocks product 0 most heavily, which is where overstocking costs the most.

So candidate 5 should have the highest expected profit, followed by candidate 3. Something slightly above 1.0× might be better still, but none of the candidates offers that.
